title: Anurag Kashyap Has a Non-Bailable Warrant Hanging Over Him — and the Story Behind It Is Messier Than You Think
excerpt: A Surat court has ordered criminal proceedings against the 'Gangs of Wasseypur' director over social media posts allegedly targeting the Brahmin community. Kashyap hasn't responded to summons.
body:
The filmmaker who built a career on confronting uncomfortable truths now finds himself on the wrong side of a legal confrontation he apparently chose to ignore.

## What Happened

A court in Surat, Gujarat, has ordered criminal proceedings against Anurag Kashyap over social media posts that allegedly defamed and incited enmity against the Brahmin community. The charges fall under Sections 196, 352, and 353(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita — roughly equivalent to promoting enmity between groups, defamation, and circulating statements conducing to public mischief.

The case originates from a complaint filed by Kamlesh Raval, a Vishva Hindu Parishad leader and lawyer, who alleges that Kashyap's posts on X (formerly Twitter) specifically targeted Brahmin community members and attempted to stoke communal hostility.

## The Phule Connection

The timeline is important. The complaint traces back to protests that erupted on April 16, 2025, around the trailer for Kashyap's film *Phule* — a biopic about social reformer Jyotirao Phule, whose legacy includes fierce criticism of the caste system and Brahminical orthodoxy. When members of the Brahmin community protested the trailer's depiction, Kashyap responded on social media with posts that Raval and his legal team characterise as deliberately inflammatory.

According to court documents, the posts weren't a one-time eruption. Raval's complaint cites posts from both 2020 and 2025, suggesting a pattern of statements that, in his legal team's reading, constitute sustained targeting of a specific community.

## The Non-Bailable Warrant

Here's where it gets serious. When the Surat court initially summoned Kashyap to respond to the complaint, he didn't appear. That silence — whether strategic, dismissive, or simply the result of bad legal advice — prompted the court to issue a non-bailable warrant.

A non-bailable warrant doesn't mean bail can't be granted; it means Kashyap can't simply walk into a police station and post bail automatically. He would need to petition the court directly, which adds both legal complexity and public spectacle to a situation he may have hoped would quietly fade.

## What the Diaspora Should Know

For NRI audiences who know Kashyap primarily through Netflix — *Sacred Games*, *Gangs of Wasseypur*, *Ugly* — this case sits at the intersection of creative expression and India's evolving legal landscape around speech. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, which replaced the colonial-era Indian Penal Code in 2024, has introduced updated provisions around hate speech and communal enmity that are still being tested in courts.

Whether Kashyap's posts constitute legitimate criticism of caste politics or cross into defamation and enmity-promotion is precisely the kind of question these new provisions were designed — for better or worse — to adjudicate.

For Indian filmmakers working internationally, the case also raises practical questions about social media risk. Kashyap is one of India's most globally recognised directors, a fixture at international film festivals and a symbol of India's independent cinema movement. A non-bailable warrant, regardless of its eventual outcome, carries reputational weight that travels across borders.

## What Happens Next

Kashyap has not publicly commented on the warrant. His legal team will need to engage with the Surat court to either quash the proceedings or secure bail — a process that could stretch across months. Meanwhile, the charges stand, and the Phule controversy continues to generate debate about where artistic provocation ends and legal liability begins.

The irony is thick enough to script: the man who made *Gangs of Wasseypur* — a film about cycles of violence and the impossibility of escaping consequences — may have just discovered that social media posts carry their own kind of long-tailed karma.

*Sources: Bollywood Hungama, Zoom TV Entertainment, Global India Broadcast News, The Popular Story, Press Post*
